what: Resource hints tell the browser what it will need before it discovers it: preload for critical files on this page, preconnect for a server you will call soon, and prefetch or Speculation Rules for the next page. Done well, navigations feel instant; done carelessly, they waste bandwidth.
like: Like a waiter who lays the cutlery and pours water before you order, and quietly preheats the dessert when you glance at the menu's last page.
why: Critical files (hero image, font, key chunk) start downloading earlier, helping LCP
The next click can feel instant because its HTML or chunk is already fetched
Early connection setup removes DNS, TCP and TLS wait for third-party origins

steps.d: Use <link rel=preload as=...> for a late-discovered, critical resource: the LCP image behind CSS or JS, a font, or a key script chunk. as sets priority and cache matching; fonts also need crossorigin.
rel=preconnect starts DNS, TCP and TLS for an origin you will use soon (image CDN, API, font host). Do it for only a few origins; connections idle for about 10 seconds are closed.
rel=prefetch fetches at low priority for a future navigation. In a SPA, the router prefetches the next route chunk when a link is hovered or enters the viewport.
A script type=speculationrules block (or Speculation-Rules header) asks Chrome to prefetch or prerender URLs. Prerender renders the page in a hidden tab, so activation is near-instant.
immediate fires at once, eager on slight hover, moderate after about 200 ms hover, conservative on pointer down. Pick moderate for most links to avoid waste.
Defer analytics and side effects until prerender activation (document.prerendering, prerenderingchange), skip Save-Data users, and avoid prefetching logout or add-to-cart URLs.

numbers.l: Hover time before a moderate-eagerness speculation fires on desktop
Chrome's limit for conservative, moderate and eager speculations (oldest cancelled first); immediate allows 50 prefetches and 10 prerenders
After load, Chrome warns in the console about a preload that was not used
Typical cost of a DNS lookup that dns-prefetch can save

tool: Speculation Rules, link rel preload/preconnect/prefetch, framework Link prefetch

choices.d: If the LCP image is already in the HTML, fetchpriority=high is enough. Preload is for resources the parser cannot see early (CSS backgrounds, fonts, JS-injected images).
Prefetch fetches the document only (cheap, safe). Prerender also runs the page in a hidden tab (instant, but costs CPU, memory and may fire side effects). Start with prefetch.
Eager is aggressive and wasteful; conservative is safest but gives less head start. Moderate (hover) is the common balance.
Speculation Rules cover full-page navigations in Chrome and Edge only, not SPA route changes. A SPA needs router-level prefetch of its route chunk and data.

instead.why: What you prefetch in a SPA: the next route's lazy chunk
Faster first byte and progressive HTML reduce the need to guess the next page

breaks.d: Too many preloads or aggressive speculation fetch things the user never uses.
breaks.see: Console warning about unused preload; high data use
breaks.fix: Preload only the few critical files; use moderate eagerness; respect Save-Data

breaks.d: Preload without the right as or crossorigin means the browser fetches the file twice.
breaks.see: Same URL requested twice in the network tab
breaks.fix: Set as correctly; add crossorigin for fonts

breaks.d: A prerendered page fires page-view tracking or actions before the user visits.
breaks.fix: Wait for document.prerendering to end; keep prefetched URLs side-effect free

say: I preload only what the parser can't discover early, such as the LCP image behind CSS or a font, and preconnect to the image CDN.
For navigation I use Speculation Rules with moderate eagerness: prefetch first, prerender only for high-confidence links, and I keep GET URLs side-effect free.
In the SPA, the router prefetches the next route chunk on hover or when the link enters the viewport.

followups.q: What is the risk of prerendering?
followups.a: It spends CPU, memory and bandwidth, and runs page code before the user arrives. Analytics and side effects must wait for activation, and the browser treats it as a hint it may ignore.
Preload is a mandatory, high-priority fetch for the current page. Prefetch is an optional, low-priority fetch for a future navigation.

today: Speculation Rules are the modern way to prefetch and prerender whole pages in Chromium browsers (Firefox support is partial, Safari has it behind a flag), with eagerness levels and document rules. Preload, preconnect and fetchpriority remain the toolkit for the current page.

sources.t: Chrome for Developers: Prerender pages and Speculation Rules

check.q: When is preload the right tool?
check.a: A critical resource the browser discovers late (a font, or an image set in CSS)
d: A link the user might click
check.why: Preload is mandatory and high priority, so keep it for a few critical late-discovered files.

check.a: Starts DNS, TCP and TLS to an origin early
check.why: It removes connection setup time from later requests to that origin.

check.q: A downside of prerendering a page?
check.a: It uses CPU and memory and can run side effects before the user visits
d: It makes the current page slower to scroll
check.why: Prerender runs the page in the background, so analytics and side effects must wait for activation.
